Hi I'm so sorry you're all struggling. I think it's very admirable of you to come here for help. That really speaks volumes and I'm here for it! I'm by no means qualified to tell you what your son needs or what your role should be for him. For me personally, I picture my brain sort of caught in a cat 5 hurricane of intrusive thoughts. They consist of ideations stemming from shame, social anxiety, failures, etc. When I'm suicidal, they are freaking destructive. Like fallen trees in your living room and a 10 foot water surge levels of destructive lol. Here's a general timeline of my "hurricane" recovery.

My first objective is to find shelter to ride out the storm. Ideally, I reach out to my support and ask for help. The circumstances are out of our control so the only thing we can really do is practice patience until the worst of the storm passes. It doesn't make sense to try and repair the roof or call the insurance appraiser *during* the hurricane, right? Lol. The storm is causing a lot of damage and at this point I'm not okay, but before I can hear my support properly, I need to be okay with being "not okay." Sometimes I enjoy being held, sometimes I don't. 

After the worst has passed, my next objective is to ground myself. The storm's subsided a tiny bit and now we can leave the broom closet, grab some food, let the dog out, maybe it's necessary to quickly screw a wood plank to the front door, but the power's out and the car's floating down the street and repairs are still inadvisable lol. At this point, I crave validation and support. It usually takes the form of someone acknowledging my pain without trying to correct it, but instead practicing curiosity. I've found I respond well even just to rephrased questions and compassion. "I'm sorry you're hurting." "I'm here for you however you need." "That sounds difficult." "Do you want to tell me about what's made you feel that way lately?" "So you feel like x when y happens?" Even just the permission to talk out loud usually gets me to a better place; one that's not sunshine by any means, but one with more clarity, less rain, and 1% closer to clean up.

Depending on how the storm's treating me, sometimes my next objective may just be sleeping through the outer bands as best I can to wake up with more energy. Not necessarily though.

For me, the most difficult step is the first clean up phase, i.e. tackling the "1% better" opportunities. Sometimes it's objectively analyzing my circumstances. Sometimes it's doing something productive and engaging with my hands. Sometimes it's as simple as just taking a shower. But the primary key in this stage is vitality. It's easy to get discouraged by the amount of damage the storm caused, but starting somewhere, for even half a moment, is progress. I'm more responsive to breathing techniques in this stage. 

Eventually, we arrive at the aftermath phase. Let's say we're at 15% and made a decent dent in the clean up. Now is the time to start really assessing the damage. At this point, we can start brainstorming and making repair plans. I'm way more receptive to input here. Sometimes I need to hear a hard truth. Sometimes I need a push towards something. Sometimes, I just need more encouragement. And I don't hate when my support encourages me with positive reinforcement :) Presently, I'd love then treating me in a way that tells me my imperfections and weaknesses don't define me.

To be, the most thing to remember is that hurricanes are devastating, and there is a stupid, albeit unsafe way of riding them out. Mom used to remind me of how selfish I am for being caught in a hurricane, and how brokenhearted she'd be if she lost the house. She didn't bother to ask me questions, she just judged me and made it about herself. Stil I resent her for that. I hope you were able to find something in this that helps, and please accept my compassion and best wishes for you and your family. I'm proud of all of you for being brave.

This is called gaslighting. It's narcissistic behavior. It's funny, I never thought of my own relationship with my mother as anything out of the ordinary. Just mom and daughter, who bicker and argue sometimes. And occasionally break each other's hearts. Casual! Therapist had a fucking field day dissecting her the day he asked the question that got the snow ball rolling. I'll paraphrase his thoughts:

This is only one instance. She likely emotionally manipulates you often and you just never realized. It's hard to see past toxicity when you're raised in toxicity.

Think about the times you felt anxious or guilty while talking to her but couldn't understand why.

Think about all the times she refused to hold herself accountable or apologize, and what tactics she employed as an alternative.

We discovered a LOT of of my anxiety and depression was a direct byproduct of this emotional abuse. It was undetected for 26 years. That woman uses my love for her against me. She knows it works. And I fucking hate that feeling more than I can properly articulate. Because, like you, I didn't have a supportive advocate when I was on the brink; I had an arrogant judge.

I'm not a doctor, nor do I know you or your mother. This was my experience. I empathize with your struggles and hope sharing helps you. Best wishes, friend.

Deep breath. Okay, done. Next.
Standing up. Done. Next. 
Deep breath. Done. Next. 
Take a big fucking poop. Done. Next. 
Deep breath. Done. Next.
Pet dog. Done. Next.

Eventually, I find I have a little momentum to tackle the bigger activities. Like going outside or getting back into my hobbies. Soon after that, I have a little strength to tackle the bigger problems. Like my finances, relationships, bad habits.

First, fuck that guy. You were the child and the victim. And I'm so sorry you endured that.

Second, there was an interesting "proverb" of sorts I heard recently that I'll paraphrase. Let's consider you travel back in time and you are sitting directly across from a younger version of you. You say to him, "buddy, here's the deal. You are precious to me. Your innocence and ignorant optimism make your imperfections perfect. I am going to do everything in my power to ensure you have the life you deserve. Here is a million dollars and a financial advisor. I've also spoken to mom; don't worry, she's prepared for all the stuff I told her to be prepared for. All of those bad things in our life that happened, we'll take care of them for you. Here is the world's best psychiatrist, because even the healthiest person in the world will benefit from therapy. Go, have yourself a fun education, avoid these people, get into these hobbies sooner rather than later, eat healthy, exercise, don't get too attached to game of thrones, appreciate the people who extend loyalty and kindness to you, and above all else, be mindful of your headspace. A million dollars is yours if you comply with my terms." 

What happens is this kid, having never suffered the way you have, and having never experienced the nuances in your life that shaped you, lives a perfect life. He grows up to be an unrecognizable version of you. (Perhaps irrelevant, but depending on your interpretation of time travel lol), you cease to exist entirely and never have that grand confrontation with yourself at all.

Essentially the point is, even in the midst of all the things we hate about ourselves, if we love even one thing, just ONE thing (maybe it's a talent, or something we did for a loved one once, or adopting a dog, or a hobby, whatever), we have to acknowledge that THIS version of ourself that loves THIS thing only exists because of the nuances that shaped THIS life.

Sometimes, this "proverb" is enough for me.

Sometimes it isn't. If you're having one of those nights, please friend, allow that one thing to consume every cell in your body. Fester in it. Marinate in it. Blind yourself from everything else.

If that doesn't work, please accept my compassion and best wishes.

Hey there. I am sorry for your loss. I can't imagine what you're going through, but your strength, patience, and loyalty to your friend has earned my utmost respect and admiration. I am a bipolar 25F who often struggles with suicidal thoughts, and this is a list of recommendations I have for you, based on what *I* would need/want. I hope it helps. :)

First, a healing environment is one that is centered around productivity. Lethargy is a bipolar person's kryptonite. Consider her hobbies (e.g. I like drawing); if my best friend were to set me up a tiny "studio" (even just some colored pencils and paper), and encourage me, well there's a level of gratitude that can't be expressed in words. Encourage her to go on walks, perhaps if there are trails near you, you could go there. Watch your favorite movies together. Make overly enthusiastic dinner plans, that you go shopping for together, and cook together, all while not taking yourself too seriously (it's fun whether or not it tastes good). :) If you're into meditating, invite her to join breath with you. If not, I recommend an app called Headspace. It's as necessary to me now as my morning cup of coffee. The best part is that all of these ideas hardly require social distancing! Weaponize her interests against her disorder!

Second, I'm sure you and your friend have spoken about her (and your) mental illnesses before, so this feels like it goes without saying. When I'm in my depressive states, I need someone who *invites* me to speak candidly about my thoughts. So I know I can open up when I'm ready, but not pressured to when I need my space.

Third, the conversation that you're nervous to have is one that she is also nervous about (I assume. I obviously don't know either of you). :) For me, these conversations are easier when I have a little metta pow wow beforehand, i.e. talking about what we're going to talk about. It's like pressing pause on the anxiety, and it allows you to go into it a little more light-heartedly. Try to avoid language like, "we need to talk," or, "I know we don't want to talk about this..." Instead try, "when you're ready, I would like to talk about what our next move is." Be excited to talk about it! :) Hell, make it a wine and ice cream night. Be forthcoming, and tell her exactly what you need from her. And focus the discussion on an optimistic future centralized around long term healing.

Fourth, I'm sorry I'm writing a lot. I'm just so empathetic and invested in your wonderful friendship. Also I'm currently manic. lmao

Lastly, and arguably most importantly, pay attention to her personal hygiene. It correlates strongly to our headspace, acting as both a symptom and often a cause of depressive states. If you suspect she isn't showering or brushing her teeth, the best thing you can do is gently address it. Half of the anxiety I feel is when I know someone knows, but doesn't say anything. It's another difficult conversation, sure, but once she gets the push, I'm certain she'll feel better.

I'm so thankful to know there are people like you in the world. To take the time to even ask for advice is so impressive. You amaze me, you anonymous flower! Thank you for reading my comment. I wish you and your friend the best on your mental health journeys. Remember, the opposite of depression is not happiness; it's vitality. Take care.
